title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Here's today's research digest across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Each section distills recent, reputable findings from PubMed, JAMA Network, NIH/ClinicalTrials.gov, Nature, Frontiers, and clinical practice guidelines; citations are linked as chips below each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
This week's theme: the serious longevity science is still about **finding safe doses and reading biomarkers** — not proving people live longer. Two big geroscience trials are now enrolling, and urolithin A keeps building the most coherent human evidence.

- **Rapamycin, done rigorously.** The NIA-backed **RESTOR** trial (NCT06658093, UT Health San Antonio, recruiting since March 2026) is an exploratory PK/PD study testing **rapamycin (sirolimus) and everolimus** in healthy older adults to find a dose and schedule that safely lowers mTOR activity toward youthful levels — and it explicitly expects the **best dose to differ between women and men**. The parallel **RAP PAC** phase-1 study (NCT05949658, Univ. of Wisconsin, adults 55–89) is dose-finding weekly sirolimus/everolimus at 5/10/15 mg. Reality check: both exist *because* safe anti-aging dosing in humans is still unknown, and **rapamycin is prescription-only, not a supplement**.
- **Urolithin A (immune aging).** A **Nature Aging** RCT (50 healthy middle-aged adults, 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks; NCT05735886) found UA expanded **naive-like, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells** and boosted mitochondrial biogenesis and fatty-acid oxidation in immune cells — early but mechanistically clean evidence for countering "inflammaging."
- **Where the field actually stands.** A 2026 comparative review of urolithin A, spermidine, and NAD+ precursors concluded **UA has the most coherent translational profile** (mechanism + biomarker + early functional data, especially mitochondrial and muscle endurance); **NAD+ boosters (NR/NMN) reliably raise NAD-related biomarkers but haven't shown clear anti-aging benefit**; and **spermidine remains biologically plausible but clinically unvalidated**.

Practical framing: prefer interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-molecule "lifespan" claims with skepticism.

sources.title: RESTOR: Rapamycin and Everolimus Study Towards Older Rejuvenation — exploratory PK/PD study of mTOR inhibition in older adults (recruiting)
Rapalog Pharmacology (RAP PAC) Study — phase-1 dose-finding sirolimus/everolimus in adults 55–89
Effect of the mitophagy inducer urolithin A on age-related immune decline: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial
Urolithin A, Spermidine, and NAD+ Precursors in Human Healthy Aging: A Comparative Narrative Review of Recent Clinical Evidence

sections.body:
New 2026 evidence keeps HIIT as a **time-efficient cardio and heart-health tool** for women — with the recurring caveat to **add resistance work** for strength and function.

- **The big picture (meta-analysis).** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* systematic review & meta-analysis of **19 RCTs** in middle-aged and older women found HIIT **significantly improved VO2max** (SMD = 1.20; high certainty) consistently across ages and body-mass groups. But it did **not** significantly improve muscle strength, flexibility, or sit-to-stand, and walking ability was only borderline — so HIIT is a cardio intervention, not a standalone strength program.
- **Heart function.** A 2026 RCT in the *International Journal of Obesity* (women with obesity, 8 weeks of 4×4-min intervals) found **only HIIT improved myocardial efficiency** (higher global work efficiency, less wasted work) vs. moderate continuous training — suggesting an edge for reversing subclinical cardiac dysfunction.
- **Postmenopausal women.** A 2025 RCT comparing **high- vs. moderate-intensity interval walking** (10 weeks) in postmenopausal women with overweight/obesity found the high-intensity group had **superior gains in body composition, 6-minute-walk aerobic capacity, and plasma volume**. A separate 2026 *BMC Women's Health* RCT of a high-intensity functional program (8 weeks) improved physical performance and menopausal quality-of-life measures.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardiorespiratory and cardiac wins; **pair HIIT with strength training**, progress gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sources.title: Effects of HIIT on cardiopulmonary fitness and physical function in middle-aged and elderly women: a systematic review and meta-analysis (19 RCTs)

Effects of a high-intensity functional exercise program on menopausal symptoms, physical & dual-task performance in postmenopausal women: an RCT

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based, **first-line** approach for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Fresh 2026 trials sharpen *when* to start it and *what to add* when muscles are very weak.

- **Start in pregnancy to prevent leaks.** A large multicenter **JAMA Network Open** RCT (**764 first-time mothers**, 9 hospitals) found a supervised prenatal **pelvic floor workout (PEFLOW)** cut SUI at 6 weeks postpartum to **8.7% vs. 13.9%** in controls, with better muscle strength — evidence for prevention, not just treatment.
- **Try PFMT before surgery.** A 2026 *International Urogynecology Journal* RCT of **intensive 6-week preoperative PFMT** in women awaiting mid-urethral sling surgery significantly improved muscle strength and symptom severity — and **43% postponed their planned surgery**, supporting structured PFMT as a low-risk first step.
- **Very weak pelvic floor? Add stimulation.** A multicenter, double-blind RCT found adding **sEMG-triggered intravaginal electrical stimulation** to supervised PFMT produced earlier, greater, and longer-lasting gains in strength and continence (meaningful improvement in **65% vs. 18%** at 12 months) for women whose muscles are too weak for exercises alone. A separate 2026 *Scientific Reports* RCT found adding **interferential current** helped mainly by **reducing weekly leakage frequency**, with no added benefit on most other measures.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised and telehealth-guided programs both outperform education alone.

sources.title: Pelvic Floor Workout for Preventing Stress Urinary Incontinence in Primiparous Women: A Randomized Clinical Trial (PEFLOW, n=764)

Pelvic muscle training + sEMG-triggered electrostimulation for weak pelvic floor: a multicentre randomised trial
Adding interferential current to pelvic floor exercises reduces weekly frequency of stress urinary incontinence

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard HER2-targeted treatment** — not a replacement for it. TP53 (p53) status is emerging as a genuinely useful lens here, since **HER2+ tumors carry TP53 mutations 47–75% of the time** and germline TP53 carriers skew toward HER2+ disease.

- **Correct vitamin D if deficient.** A 2026 retrospective interventional study in *Nutrients* (196 curative-intent HER2+ patients) found that **failing to correct a documented vitamin D deficiency carried a ~1.7× higher recurrence risk**, with the best disease-free-survival trends in those reaching the highest levels. The authors highlight **TP53–vitamin D receptor cross-talk**: in a TP53-mutant subset of the AMATERASU trial, vitamin D drove **81% vs. 31% 5-year relapse-free survival** — hinting TP53 may flag who benefits most.
- **Supplements — mechanism vs. proof.** **Curcumin** downregulates HER2 and PI3K/Akt/NF-κB signaling in lab and xenograft models (even in trastuzumab-resistant cells), and has been paired with paclitaxel in a metastatic breast-cancer trial — but human HER2/TP53-specific efficacy is unproven, and **bioavailability and drug interactions matter**. Coordinate any supplement with your oncology team.
- **On the horizon (standard care).** Preclinical work shows **HER2;TP53 co-mutated tumors are especially sensitive to TOP1 inhibitors** — the payload class inside **trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd)** — and that **neratinib + T-DXd act synergistically**. That combination is now in a phase-1 trial (NCT05372614). Separately, 2026 data confirm **PIK3CA mutations blunt response** to dual HER2 blockade, reinforcing genomic testing to guide therapy.

Important framing: much of this is **early, observational, or preclinical**. Use integrative options as **add-ons discussed with an oncologist** — never as substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy.

sources.title: Successful Vitamin D Replacement After Deficiency and Disease-Free Survival in Curative-Intent HER2+ Breast Cancer: A Retrospective Interventional Study
The Potential Utility of Curcumin in HER-2-Overexpressed Breast Cancer: In Vitro and In Vivo Comparison with Herceptin
HER2; p53 Co-mutated Cancers Show Increased Histone Acetylation and are Sensitive to Neratinib plus Trastuzumab Deruxtecan

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or **fragmented (waking-through-the-night)** sleep, 2025–2026 guidance is consistent: **behavioral therapy first, pills second, supplements last**.

- **CBT-I is first-line — and best for fragmentation.** The 2025 **VA/DoD clinical practice guideline** gives CBT-I a **strong** recommendation over medication, and recommends **against sleep-hygiene advice as a stand-alone**. The single most effective component for disjointed sleep is **sleep restriction / consolidation**: fix a wake time, limit time in bed to your actual sleep time (+~30 min), and build sleep drive to **reduce night-time awakenings**.
- **If you need medication, favor the newer class.** Both the VA/DoD 2025 guideline and the European Insomnia Guideline list **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** — daridorexant, lemborexant, suvorexant — as good options, especially for **sleep-maintenance** insomnia, alongside **low-dose doxepin**; Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone, zaleplon) remain **short-term (≤4 weeks)** choices with complex-behavior warnings.
- **Supplements, honestly.** **Melatonin** is only modestly useful and mainly for **circadian problems** (jet lag, shift work) or adults ≥55 using **prolonged-release** forms; **fast-release melatonin is not recommended** for chronic insomnia. For **magnesium**, guidelines find **insufficient evidence** to recommend for or against.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If fragmented sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to **rule out sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).

sources.title: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder (2025): CBT-I first-line; DORAs, doxepin, Z-drugs; magnesium insufficient evidence
The European Insomnia Guideline: update on diagnosis and treatment of insomnia (CBT-I first-line; orexin antagonists; melatonin limits)
Treatment of Chronic Insomnia in Adults (sleep restriction as the most effective CBT-I component; DORAs for sleep maintenance)
